new_groups.label: Congress and the President honour Washington, December 1799 to January 1800
new_groups.definition: Two documents on the honours paid to George Washington, who died on 14 December 1799, as the 1800 papers printed them: the joint resolutions of Congress of 23 December 1799, and the President's message of 8 January 1800 sending Congress Mrs. Washington's answer. Contains those two groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1800 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The joint resolutions of Congress of 23 December 1799 on the death of Washington
new_groups.definition: Printings of the resolutions that the joint committee of Congress reported through Mr. Marshall and both houses passed: 'That a Marble Monument be erected by the United States, in the Capitol, at the City of Washington, and that the family of General Washington be requested to permit his body to be deposited under it'; that there be a funeral procession and an oration before both houses on 26 December; that the people be recommended to wear crape on the left arm for thirty days; that the President send a copy to Mrs. Washington; and that he issue a proclamation. The weekly papers printed them in January 1800 with the proceedings; three papers printed them again from July to October among the laws and resolutions of the session. Congress's own resolutions.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1800 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The President's message of 8 January 1800 with Mrs. Washington's letter
new_groups.definition: Printings of the President's message to both houses, sent on 8 January 1800: 'In compliance with the request in one of the resolutions of Congress of the 21st of December last, I transmitted a copy of those resolutions, by my secretary, Mr. Shaw, to Mrs. Washington', with her answer from Mount Vernon of 31 December 1799: 'Taught by the great example which I have so long had before me, never to oppose my private wishes to the public will—I must consent to the request made by Congress'. The President's message and Mrs. Washington's letter, in their own words.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1800 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The convention of October 1799 between the Duke of York and General Brune for the British and Russian army to leave Holland
new_groups.definition: Printings of the articles 'agreed upon between Major General Knox, duly authorised by his Royal Highness the Duke of York, Commander in Chief of the combined English and Russian Army, and Citizen Rostollant ... duly authorised by Citizen Brune, General and Commander in Chief of the French and Batavian Armies' (the names vary from paper to paper): 'From the date of this convention, all hostilities shall cease between the two armies'; the combined army 'shall evacuate the territory, coasts, islands, and internal navigation of the Dutch Republic, by the 30th of November, 1799', and 'Eight thousand prisoners of war, French and Batavians ... now detained in England, shall be restored'. The London Gazette of 26 October 1799 published it with the Duke of York's dispatch of 20 October, and most papers printed the two together; the Portland Gazette printed the articles alone. The two commanders' agreement, as the British government published it.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1800 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Congress asks for the papers on a seaman delivered to the British under the 27th article of the treaty, February 1800

new_groups.definition: Printings of the President's speech to both houses in the Senate chamber on 22 November 1800: 'Immediately after the adjournment of Congress, at their last session in Philadelphia, I gave directions, in compliance with the laws, for the removal of the public offices, records and property'; it speaks of the new seat of government, the District of Columbia, the convention with France, the army and navy, and the finances. The President's own speech.

new_groups.label: Salem, December 1800: the ship Brutus brings word that the Dey of Algiers made the frigate George Washington carry his presents to Constantinople
new_groups.definition: Printings of a report from Salem, Massachusetts, headed 'Latest from Algiers and Gibraltar' in several papers: the ship Brutus, William Brown, commander, had arrived in 32 days from Gibraltar and 40 from Algiers, and 'Capt. Brown informs, that the United States frigate George Washington, capt. Bainbridge, sailed for Constantinople the 19th of Oct. having on board the Algerine General of Marine and suite, with presents, &c. for the Grand Seignior'; by the captain's account the Dey compelled Captain Bainbridge to do so and threatened war if he refused. Most papers go on with the captain's news of Lord Keith's fleet, and seven add a 'Sketch of Algerine Spoliations for the last two years'. The New Hampshire Gazette prints another Salem account of the arrival, dated 12 December, in other words ('By the information of Capt. Brown, it appears that the American Consul and flag are treated with more respect by the Dey of Algiers, than any European nation whatever'), followed by the same paragraphs; it is counted with the others as a printed form of the report. A ship captain's report at second hand.

new_groups.label: The King's speech to Parliament, 11 November 1800
new_groups.definition: Printings of the speech with which King George III opened Parliament on 11 November 1800: 'My tender concern for the welfare of my Subjects, and a sense of the difficulties with which the poorer classes particularly have to struggle, from the present high price of provisions, have induced me to call you together at an earlier period than I had otherwise intended'; it speaks of the scarcity of grain, the negotiations for peace, and the war. The papers give two different introductions. The King's own speech.

new_groups.label: The convention between France and the United States, signed 30 September 1800
new_groups.definition: Printings of the text of the convention signed at Paris on 30 September 1800 by the French plenipotentiaries and the American envoys, before the Senate had acted on it, in two translations. Six papers print the one that begins 'The First Consul of the French Republic, in the name of the French people, and the President of the United States of America, equally animated with a desire to put an end to the differences which have arisen between the two States' and whose first article reads 'There shall be a firm, inviolable and universal peace' (the National Intelligencer gives its opening in somewhat different words: 'The Premier Consul of the French Republic in the name of the people of France, and the President of the United States of America, equally desirous to terminate the differences'); the Alexandria Advertiser and the Virginia Argus print another, from the Paris papers, whose first article reads 'There shall be a sincere and universal Peace, and inviolable Friendship between the two countries'. Counted together as one item in two printed forms. The two governments' agreement, as printed before ratification.

dispositions_summary.method: The automatic families first printed in 1800 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 1,473 items printed somewhere; by the finder's count, the Gazette of the United States's two catalogue numbers taken as one paper, 7 reach 9 papers, 14 reach 8, 33 reach 7 and 88 reach 6). The same script was run with year 1799 over the 1800 pages (items_from_1799.json: 49 items, one in 7 papers and one in 6). Every item in 6 or more papers was read on its pages or checked for a seventh paper by machine (about 220 words of its text compared with every page of the year), and every item that might reach 7 was counted again by its own words with phrase searches over all 2,575 pages in both transcriptions, reading every hit.
dispositions_summary.selection_rule: The one admission rule (R-01), as for 1776, 1805, 1806, 1807, 1808 and 1809: every single printed item in 9 or more newspapers is admitted, except digests; items in 7 or 8 papers are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news; items are counted one by one; a sub-story may have fewer papers when its parent reaches 7. No year-specific threshold: items of 1800 reach 7, 8 and 9 papers. In 1800, 6 to 10 papers are in print in any three weeks (7 for most of the year), so from February to July an item in 7 papers was printed by every paper that survives for its weeks; no item first printed in May or June reaches 7. Where several items of one affair reach the band in the same weeks, the most widely printed is chosen and the others are listed as not chosen, unless they are separate public acts (the President's speech and each house's address and his replies). Nothing is held back for its subject.
dispositions_summary.paper_counting: The Gazette of the United States has two catalogue numbers in 1800 (sn83025881 to 7 May, sn84026272 from 1 July): one paper, counted once (C-04). The Ulster County Gazette of 4 January 1800 has seven scanned pages: pages 5 to 7 are a second copy of pages 1, 2 and 4 (C-05); no admitted printing stands on that issue.

counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: Counted item by item, five items of 1800 reach 9 papers: the Senate's address of 25 November, the President's reply to it, the House's address and the President's reply to it, and the Salem report of the ship Brutus (9 with the New Hampshire Gazette's other account of the same arrival, 8 in one wording). Eight reach 8: the convention for the evacuation of Holland, the letter from Constantinople on Kleber, the report of floods in China, Lord Whitworth's convention with Denmark, the President's speech of 22 November, the King's speech of 11 November, the convention with France (two translations) and the Mortefontaine entertainment (two forms). Twenty-two reach 7. Every other item is in 6 papers or fewer by its own words.
counted_item_by_item.Joins made by the finder: The finder chains the acts of the first session of the Sixth Congress through their enacting formula, signatures and titles (items of up to 91 printings), the Washington resolutions with the proclamations that recite them, and the paragraphs of one run of London news (Kleber, Canton, the Brest fleet, Munich). Each text was counted by its own words: no act reaches 7 papers (six papers printed the laws of the session; the Portland Gazette printed few federal acts); the President's proclamation on mourning is in 6 papers, the joint resolutions it recites in 7.
counted_item_by_item.Pages that only quote or summarise an it: Not counted: the Republican Ledger of 29 January, which summarises the Consuls' proclamation of 12 November 1799 ('In one of the Paris Journals it is asserted that the Constitution of the third year has perished'); the New Hampshire Gazette of 30 December, which summarises the navy pension report; the National Intelligencer of 31 December, whose debate on the mausoleum bill quotes the monument resolution; the proclamation of 6 January, which recites the resolution for 22 February.
counted_item_by_item.Printed again: A paper that printed an item again counts each printing (C-08): the joint resolutions of 23 December 1799 were printed again among the laws and resolutions of the session by the Gazette of the United States (22 July), the Providence Journal (10 September), the Oracle (11 October) and the Kentucky Gazette (13 October); the Kentucky Gazette printed the Ratisbon report on 6 and 13 October.
counted_item_by_item.Printed forms counted together: One item printed in different wordings counts as one (C-02): the convention with France in two translations (6 + 2 papers); Melas's letter in two translations; the King's speech with two introductions; the Salem report of the Brutus, where the New Hampshire Gazette prints another Salem account of the arrival in other words and goes on with the same paragraphs; the Mortefontaine report in two translations (not chosen). Two different reports of one event are not counted together when they share no text: the frigate Boston's arrival with the French corvette Berceau is in 6 papers in one report, and a seventh paper prints a different one.
counted_item_by_item.Paragraphs of the proceedings: Mr. Livingston's resolutions of 3 February 1800 reached the papers inside their reports of the House's proceedings; each such paragraph is counted as an item by its own words, as 1806 counted Mr. Gregg's resolution, 1809 Mr. Giles's and the 1804 review the paragraphs of the daily proceedings (X-1804-04); the day's proceedings as a whole stay a digest. The House's resolutions on Mr. Randolph's letter (7) and the paragraph on the House's first sitting in Washington (7) are counted the same way and not chosen.
